patients.summary: Construction site supervisor with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and old gout who joins in 2019. A stage IA nodular melanoma of the upper back is excised in 2021, lisinopril causes a cough and is replaced by hydrochlorothiazide, he completes a blood pressure drug trial, has an ED-diagnosed gout flare in 2024 and a drained parapneumonic effusion in 2025. A week after his last practice visit in June 2026 he is found to have a glioblastoma, resected and now in chemoradiation.

documents.title: New patient call
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Caller would like to transfer his primary care here; his longtime doctor's office is closing to adult patients. Works as a site supervisor for a commercial builder, prefers early morning appointments. Has diabetes and is on 'a couple of pills.' New patient visit booked 9/10 at 7:30. Release form emailed for his old office's records.

conditions.label: Gout
conditions.note: a few flares years ago; none recently

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth twice daily with meals

procedures.procedure: Office visit, new patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
53-year-old man transferring care; prior PCP's office is closing its adult panel.

Diabetes: told he had type 2 diabetes around 2013. Tried diet for a while, then metformin, now 1000 mg twice a day. Doesn't check sugars at home. No hypoglycemia. Last A1c 'around 7' per him.
Blood pressure: flagged as high about three years ago. He was asked to cut salt and lose weight and never started a pill. No home cuff.
Cholesterol: atorvastatin 40 mg for years, no muscle aches.
Gout: two or three attacks in his forties, big toe each time, treated short-term. Nothing in years and never on a daily gout medicine.

PSH: none.
Allergies: sulfa antibiotic gave him a rash as a young adult.
Family: father with type 2 diabetes, mother with high blood pressure, a brother with melanoma.
Social: married. Supervises commercial construction sites, outdoors most of the day. Never a smoker. Does not drink.

ROS otherwise negative.

Exam: well-appearing, BP and weight as charted. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft. Feet: intact skin, monofilament sensation normal, DP pulses 2+ both sides. No tophi on hands, elbows or ears.

A/P
1. Type 2 diabetes on metformin: A1c, CMP, urine microalbumin today. Eye exam due; given optometry list.
2. Hypertension, lifestyle only: pressure is borderline today. Recheck at next visit before deciding on a drug.
3. Hyperlipidemia: continue atorvastatin 40; lipids today.
4. Gout, quiet for years: no treatment.
5. Prevention: one-time hep C and HIV screens today. Will get colonoscopy and vaccine history from his old office. Flu shot next month when stock arrives.
Follow-up about 5 months.

documents.title: Lab results released
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Scott, your labs are back. Your A1c is right about where we want it on metformin. Kidney and liver numbers are normal, cholesterol is well controlled on atorvastatin, urine protein screen is normal, and the hepatitis C and HIV screens are negative. Nothing to change.

documents.title: Records from prior primary care office
documents.author: front desk
documents.body:
Received 38 pages from his previous primary care office, covering 2012 to 2019. Abstracted by RN:
- Type 2 diabetes listed since 2013; metformin titrated to 1000 mg twice daily by 2015.
- Elevated blood pressure noted from 2016, lifestyle advice, no medication.
- Atorvastatin 40 mg since 2014.
- Gout flares 2009 and 2011, treated with short courses; no maintenance therapy.
- Screening colonoscopy 2017-03: normal to the terminal ileum, no polyps; 10-year interval advised.
- Tdap 04/2017.
- Sulfonamide antibiotic allergy (rash).
Filed to media; immunization entered.

documents.title: Immunization
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Quadrivalent flu vaccine 0.5 mL IM left deltoid. VIS given. No egg or vaccine reactions in the past. Waited 15 minutes, no issues.

documents.title: Optometry diabetic eye exam letter
documents.author: optometry
documents.body: Dilated diabetic eye examination performed 01/21/2020. Visual acuity 20/20 OD, 20/25 OS with current glasses. Intraocular pressures normal. Lens clear. Fundus: no diabetic retinopathy either eye, no macular edema. Recommend repeat dilated exam in 12 months.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, low MDM

documents.title: Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:

O: BP as charted, a touch above goal again. Lungs clear, heart regular. Feet unremarkable.
A/P: Diabetes - A1c today. BP - borderline on two visits; he would rather keep working on diet and activity before a pill. Reasonable for now; recheck in a few months. Eye exam done in January, no retinopathy.

Exam: BP as charted. Heart and lungs normal. Foot exam: normal sensation to monofilament, pulses palpable.

Plan: A1c, CMP and lipids today. Home pressures are borderline; continue lifestyle and keep logging. First Shingrix dose today, second in 2-6 months. Annual physical in the spring.

orders.reason: changing pigmented lesion, upper back; brother with melanoma

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
55 yo here for his yearly exam. Feels well.

One new item: his wife has been after him about a mole in the middle of his upper back. She says it has gotten bigger and darker since late last fall. He can't see it himself. No bleeding or itch. He's shirtless or in a t-shirt on site much of the summer and doesn't use sunscreen. Brother had a melanoma removed.

No chest pain, no shortness of breath, no urinary symptoms. No gout flares.
Meds: metformin 1000 BID, atorvastatin 40. Allergy: sulfa (rash).

Exam: vitals as charted. HEENT normal. Neck supple, no nodes. Heart RRR. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, non-tender. Skin: about 1 cm pigmented lesion on the upper back left of midline with uneven color and an irregular edge; no other lesions of concern on a full skin check. No axillary or cervical adenopathy. Feet normal.

A/P
- Changing pigmented lesion, upper back, with a family history of melanoma: referred to dermatology, asked for a prompt slot.
- Diabetes: labs today including urine microalbumin.
- Hypertension: pressure still drifting above goal; we'll talk again once labs are back.
- Hyperlipidemia: lipids today.
- Prevention: colonoscopy 2017 normal, Tdap 2017, Shingrix done, COVID series done. Sunscreen and a hat on site.

documents.title: Your physical labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Scott, most of your labs look good: A1c is steady, cholesterol is well controlled and kidney function is normal. One new finding: the urine test for protein came back at 168, which is higher than it should be (under 30). That can be an early sign of strain on the kidneys from diabetes and blood pressure. I'd like to repeat it in a few months to make sure it's real. The dermatology office should call you this week; if you don't hear by Friday let us know.

documents.title: Dermatology consultation
documents.author: dermatology
documents.body:
Outside dermatology group. Visit date 06/14/2021.

Thank you for sending Mr. Dion, a 55-year-old construction supervisor, for a pigmented lesion of the upper back that has changed over roughly half a year. He is anxious about it given skin cancer in his family (a brother treated for melanoma). The site is exposed for much of his outdoor workday.

He has diabetes on metformin and takes atorvastatin; blood pressure is managed with diet. Allergy: sulfonamide antibiotics (rash). He reports no fevers, weight loss or night sweats.

Exam: Fitzpatrick type II. On the left upper back there is a 1.0 cm pigmented papule, asymmetric, with irregular borders and color ranging from brown to black. Dermoscopy: irregular streaks at the periphery and a blue-white veil centrally. No other atypical lesions on full skin exam. No palpable cervical, axillary or supraclavicular lymph nodes.

Impression: lesion highly suspicious for melanoma.

Plan: excisional biopsy with narrow margins done today under local anesthesia; layered closure, sutures out in 14 days. We will call him with pathology and plan definitive treatment from there.

reports.text: Specimen: skin, left upper back, excision. Gross: ellipse of skin 2.4 x 1.4 cm with a 1.0 cm pigmented lesion. Microscopic: invasive malignant melanoma, nodular type. Tumor thickness 0.7 mm. Ulceration absent. Dermal mitotic rate 2 per square millimeter. No lymphovascular or perineural invasion identified. Microsatellites absent. Peripheral and deep margins free of tumor; closest margin under 2 mm.
reports.conclusion: Malignant melanoma, nodular type, 0.7 mm thick, non-ulcerated, margins clear but narrow (pT1a). Wide re-excision recommended.

documents.title: Dermatopathology report received
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Pathology from the dermatology biopsy of 6/14 faxed by the dermatology office. Routed to PCP.

documents.title: Call re: melanoma pathology
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Called Scott after reading the pathology. Dermatology had already spoken with him and he has the wider excision scheduled for July 13. Thin, early melanoma; explained that the wider excision is usually all that's needed at this depth and that he'll have regular skin checks with dermatology. Wife on the line too, many questions answered. Reminded him about sun protection at work.

documents.title: Repeat microalbumin
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Urine albumin/creatinine 192, second abnormal value after 168 in May. Persistent albuminuria. Kidney function and potassium normal. Will discuss an ACE inhibitor at his October visit.

procedures.procedure: Wide local excision of skin lesion
Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Interval: had the wide excision on his upper back July 13 at the dermatology office. He says they told him the margins were clean and nothing else was left. We never received the operative or pathology note; front desk to request. Scar healed. First skin check with dermatology is in the new year.

BP today 144/90; recheck after 5 minutes similar. Home readings in the high 130s to 140s. Urine microalbumin abnormal twice (168, 192). Feels fine.

Exam: heart regular, lungs clear, no edema. Upper back scar well healed, no nodules, no axillary nodes.

A/P
1. Hypertension, no longer controlled with lifestyle, now with persistent albuminuria in a diabetic: start lisinopril 20 mg daily for pressure and kidney protection. BMP in 2-3 weeks. Explained the common side effects including a dry cough.
2. Diabetes: A1c in September at goal. Continue metformin.
3. Melanoma, stage IA, post wide excision: dermatology surveillance.
4. Flu shot and COVID booster given today.

documents.title: BMP
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Creatinine and potassium unchanged after starting lisinopril. Continue.

conditions.label: Adverse effect of ACE inhibitor (lisinopril cough)

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth every morning

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Acute visit - cough
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Came in after work. Three weeks of a dry, tickly cough that goes on through the day and is worst once he lies down at night; his wife is sleeping in the other room. Nothing comes up. No fever or chills, no chest pain, no wheeze, no shortness of breath, no runny nose or sore throat beforehand. Started lisinopril 20 mg on 10/19, so this began about six weeks in.

T 36.8, BP 136/88, P 78, sat as charted. Throat clear. Lungs clear throughout, no wheeze. Heart regular, no murmur.
UA today: protein 2+. BMP: creatinine and potassium normal.

A/P
Cough from lisinopril - classic timing and character, exam normal. Stop lisinopril; ACE-inhibitor intolerance added to allergies. Cough may take a few weeks to fade.
Hypertension: start hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg each morning.
Albuminuria: protein again on today's UA; recheck urine microalbumin with spring labs.
Call if cough persists beyond a month after stopping.

documents.title: Cough
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Cough is pretty much gone, took about 2 and a half weeks after I stopped the lisinopril. New water pill is fine, I just pee more in the morning. Home BP mostly 134/84 range.

documents.title: RE: Cough
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Great news. Those home numbers are reasonable. Keep the hydrochlorothiazide and we'll check labs before your March visit.

documents.title: Dermatology follow-up
documents.author: dermatology
documents.body: Melanoma surveillance visit 02/08/2022. History of stage IA nodular melanoma, left upper back, treated with wide local excision 07/2021. He has no new or changing spots. Full-body skin exam: excision scar well healed with no pigment or nodularity; scattered benign nevi and seborrheic keratoses; no suspicious lesions. No lymphadenopathy in the cervical, axillary or inguinal basins. Plan: skin checks every 6 months for the first 2 years, then yearly. Daily sunscreen and protective clothing at work.

events.reason: follow-up; asks about a blood pressure drug trial

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Here for routine follow-up, about three months after the lisinopril cough and nine months out from the melanoma. Cough long gone. Taking hydrochlorothiazide, metformin and atorvastatin.

He saw an ad from a university research clinic recruiting for a study of a new blood pressure medicine and has the information packet with him. Wants to know whether it's worth signing up and what the downsides are. No chest pain, no breathlessness, no leg swelling.

BP 138/86, HR 78. Heart and lungs normal. No edema. Exam otherwise unremarkable.

Labs 3/8: fasting glucose 146, A1c 7.2, creatinine 1.1, potassium 4.5, LDL 98. Urine microalbumin still elevated.

A/P
1. Hypertension on HCTZ, close to goal. Went through the packet with him: it is a randomized, blinded study comparing an investigational pill with an approved drug, added to his current medicine, with visits at the research site every few months for about a year. Talked through the possible upside (closer monitoring, maybe better control) and downside (unknown side effects, extra visits, he won't know which drug he's on). He wants to enroll. I'm fine with it; he'll keep us updated and we'll keep managing his diabetes and cholesterol here. Signed release so the site can get his records.
2. Diabetes: A1c 7.2, continue metformin.
3. Lipids at goal on atorvastatin 40.
4. Melanoma: dermatology skin check in February was clear.
Follow-up in about 6 months.

documents.title: Clinical trial enrollment notice
documents.author: research site
documents.body:
University clinical research unit - participant enrollment notice to primary care physician.

Your patient Scott Dion consented and was randomized today in a double-blind, active-controlled study of an investigational antihypertensive agent. He will take one blinded study tablet daily in addition to his current regimen. Seated baseline blood pressure at today's screening visit: 154/96 mmHg (mean of three readings). Study visits are scheduled at months 1, 3, 6, 9 and 11. Please do not change his antihypertensive medications without contacting the study coordinator unless clinically necessary. A 24-hour line for study questions is on the participant's wallet card. Study coordinator phone: 413-555-0187.

documents.title: Refill request
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Pharmacy refill request for metformin 1000 mg and atorvastatin 40 mg, 90-day supply each. Last labs March. Approved per protocol with 3 refills.

documents.title: Dermatology follow-up
documents.author: dermatology
documents.body: Six-month skin surveillance 08/16/2022. No new concerns. Scar on left upper back flat and pale, no recurrence. Full skin exam without atypical lesions. Nodes negative. Continue every 6 months through mid-2023, then annually.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Six months into the BP study. Hasn't missed a study pill or his hydrochlorothiazide, keeps a pill box in the truck. The coordinator told him his numbers have come down since he started. No dizziness, no new symptoms.

BP 128/82 today, nicely controlled. Heart regular, lungs clear, no edema. Foot exam normal.

Labs 8/30: fasting glucose 98, A1c 6.8, total cholesterol 180, LDL 95, creatinine 1.0, potassium 4.5.

A/P
HTN: well controlled on HCTZ plus blinded study drug. No changes; study manages its own drug.
DM: A1c 6.8, nice improvement. Continue metformin.
Lipids: at goal.
Flu and the new bivalent COVID booster plus pneumococcal vaccine at a nurse visit next month.
See him after the study wraps up.

documents.title: Immunizations
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Three vaccines today: flu (L deltoid), bivalent COVID booster (R deltoid), PCV20 for diabetes (R deltoid, separate site). VIS sheets given. Observed 15 minutes, fine.

documents.title: Study completion notice
documents.author: research site
documents.body: University clinical research unit - end-of-study notice. Mr. Dion completed all study visits per protocol; his final visit was 02/14/2023 and blinded study medication was stopped that day. He remains on his pre-study regimen. Treatment assignment stays blinded until the study database is locked; participants and physicians will receive a plain-language results summary when available. Thank you for supporting his participation.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Finished the BP study last month. Feels good, taking everything as prescribed. He heard from others in the waiting room at the site that a fair number of people quit early because of side effects, though nobody knew which arm they were in. The summary sheet the site mailed out says the two drugs ended up about the same for blood pressure. He's glad he did it.

BP 132/84. Exam unremarkable: heart regular, lungs clear, no edema, feet normal.

Labs 2/28: fasting glucose 138, A1c 7.2, creatinine 1.1, LDL 98.

A/P
- HTN on hydrochlorothiazide alone again, acceptable.
- DM: A1c 7.2, back up a little from the fall. Talked about portion sizes in the truck. Continue metformin.
- Hyperlipidemia: continue atorvastatin.
- Eye exam due; reminded.
Physical in June.

documents.body: Diabetic eye examination 04/04/2023, dilated. Best corrected acuity 20/20 each eye. No diabetic retinopathy in either eye; maculae flat and dry. Early lens changes, not visually significant. Return in one year.

documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
57-year-old for his physical. Busy season, two sites going at once. Lost a couple of pounds since spring. No complaints. No gout flares. Dermatology checks have all been clean.

Meds: metformin 1000 BID, hydrochlorothiazide 25 daily, atorvastatin 40 daily.
Allergies: sulfonamide antibiotics (rash); ACE inhibitors (cough).

Exam: vitals as charted. Eyes, ears, throat normal. Neck without nodes or thyroid enlargement. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, no masses. Skin: back scar fine, no new lesions I can see. Feet: monofilament intact, pulses good, no calluses. Mood good.

Plan: CMP, CBC, lipids, A1c. Colonoscopy not due until 2027. Vaccines current; flu and COVID in the fall. Keep up sunscreen at work.

documents.title: Dermatology follow-up
documents.author: dermatology
documents.body: Annual-interval skin check 08/08/2023 for history of stage IA melanoma, upper back, excised 2021. No new or changing lesions reported or found. Scar intact. Nodal basins negative. Moving to yearly full-skin exams.

Yearly visit. Feeling well, no new problems. Taking metformin, HCTZ and atorvastatin daily. Skin check with dermatology last August was clean.

ROS negative across systems.

Exam: vitals as charted. Head and neck normal. Heart regular. Lungs clear. Abdomen benign. Skin without new pigmented lesions; back scar fine. Feet: sensation and pulses normal. Joints: no swelling, no tophi.

events.reason: right great toe pain and swelling

conditions.label: Acute gout flare, right first MTP joint

medications.sig: Take 2 tablets now and 1 tablet one hour later, then 1 tablet twice daily until the flare settles

reports.text: Specimen: synovial fluid, right first metatarsophalangeal joint. Appearance cloudy, yellow. Nucleated cells 18,000/mm3, neutrophils 75%. Gram stain: no organisms seen. Crystal exam under polarized light: needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals, intracellular and extracellular. Culture: no growth.
reports.conclusion: Inflammatory fluid with monosodium urate crystals; no organisms.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Area hospital emergency department. Seen 06/09/2024.

CC: right big toe pain x 2 days.

HPI: 58M with diabetes, hypertension, high cholesterol and prior gout, now in a blood pressure study per his old records, though he says he finished it. Throbbing pain in the right great toe that woke him two nights ago, came on fast, with redness and swelling since. Can't fit a work boot. Denies any injury.

Meds per patient: hydrochlorothiazide, metformin. Home list from prior visit: lisinopril 20 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg.
Allergies: ACE inhibitors (cough), sulfa drugs (rash).
Family: brother melanoma; father T2DM; mother HTN.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol; construction site supervisor.

Exam: vitals reviewed, afebrile. Right 1st MTP red, hot and exquisitely tender; motion limited by pain. Remainder of exam unremarkable.

Procedure: right 1st MTP arthrocentesis after informed consent, sterile prep, 25-gauge needle, small volume cloudy fluid. Tolerated well.

Results: synovial WBC 18,000 with 75% neutrophils; Gram stain negative; needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals.

MDM: crystal-proven acute gout. No features of septic joint on fluid or exam. Renal function normal on recent outpatient labs per patient portal.

Disposition: home. Colchicine 1.2 mg now and 0.6 mg in one hour, then 0.6 mg twice daily until the flare settles. Ice, elevation. Follow up with PCP this week.

documents.title: Gout
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Went to the ER yesterday, right big toe blew up. They stuck a needle in it and said gout crystals. Gave me colchicine. They said to see you this week. Can I get in Thursday early?

documents.title: RE: Gout
documents.author: front desk

Seen in the ED Sunday for a red, swollen right great toe; per him the tap showed gout crystals. ED record not here yet. Started colchicine there; some loose stools yesterday, otherwise tolerating. Pain about a third of what it was, back in a sneaker.

Exam: afebrile. Right 1st MTP mildly warm and swollen, much less tender, can flex it. No other joints involved.

A/P
Acute gout, right great toe, crystal-confirmed per patient, improving. Continue colchicine until fully settled, then stop; if diarrhea worsens drop to once daily. Stay hydrated on hot job sites. Continue hydrochlorothiazide and other meds. Call if another flare.

events.reason: shortness of breath and cough after pneumonia

conditions.label: Community-acquired pneumonia
conditions.note: treated at urgent care with an oral antibiotic

reports.text: PA and lateral chest. Moderate left pleural effusion layering to occupy roughly one third of the left hemithorax, with blunting of the costophrenic angle and adjacent compressive atelectasis. No mediastinal shift. Right lung clear. Heart size normal.

Specimen: pleural fluid, left, diagnostic thoracentesis. Appearance: hazy, straw-colored. pH 7.36. Glucose 112 mg/dL. LDH 310 U/L (serum LDH 190 U/L). Protein 3.9 g/dL (serum protein 6.8 g/dL). Nucleated cells 3,200/uL, neutrophil predominant. Gram stain: no organisms seen. Culture: no growth at 5 days (final). Cytology: negative for malignant cells.
reports.conclusion: Exudate by protein and LDH ratios; pH and glucose not in the complicated range; Gram stain and culture negative.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional medical center ED. Date of service 06/02/2025.

Chief complaint: worsening shortness of breath and dry cough for a week, worse lying down.

HPI: 59-year-old man with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and gout. Had a lisinopril-related cough back in 2021. Diagnosed with a left-sided pneumonia at an urgent care about two weeks ago and finished the oral antibiotic he was given. Over the past week has become more short of breath, has a nagging dry cough and is wiped out; breathing is harder when he lies flat. No other recent illness. Never smoked. Denies fever, chest pain or coughing blood.

Home medications (from prior record): metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily.
Allergies: ACE inhibitors (cough intolerance), sulfa drugs (rash).
FHx: brother melanoma, father T2DM, mother HTN.

Exam: RR 22, SpO2 94% RA, afebrile, BP and HR within normal limits; mildly tachypneic, hemodynamically stable, speaking full sentences. Left lower chest: reduced breath sounds, dull to percussion, decreased tactile fremitus. Right lung clear. Heart regular. No leg edema.

CXR: moderate left effusion, about a third of the hemithorax.

Procedure: diagnostic thoracentesis, left midaxillary line, needle passed over the upper border of the rib below the chosen interspace, after consent and local anesthesia. Fluid sent. No complications; post-procedure film without pneumothorax.

MDM: effusion following a recent pneumonia. Fluid results consistent with an uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion. Given size and symptoms, discussed with hospitalist and pulmonary: admit for IV antibiotics and drainage.

Disposition: admitted to medicine.

medications.drug: amoxicillin 875 MG / clavulanate 125 MG Oral Tablet
medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth twice daily for 7 days

reports.text: Portable AP chest after left small-bore pleural catheter placement. Catheter tip projects over the left lower hemithorax. Left effusion substantially smaller. No pneumothorax. Right lung clear.
reports.conclusion: Left pleural catheter in place, effusion decreased, no pneumothorax.

reports.text: Portable AP chest following removal of left pleural catheter. Minimal residual blunting of the left costophrenic angle. No pneumothorax.
reports.conclusion: Catheter removed, no pneumothorax, trace residual fluid.

procedures.procedure: Hospital discharge day management, 30 minutes or less

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: hospitalist
documents.body:
Admitted 06/02/2025, discharged 06/06/2025. Hospital medicine service.

Diagnoses: uncomplicated parapneumonic effusion, left, following community-acquired pneumonia. Type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, gout (history).

Course: admitted from the ED after diagnostic thoracentesis showed an exudative effusion with pH 7.36, glucose 112, LDH 310 and negative Gram stain; culture later finalized as no growth and cytology negative. Started on IV ampicillin-sulbactam. Because the effusion was moderate and he was breathless, interventional pulmonology placed a small-bore chest tube on 6/3, draining about 1,100 mL over two days with steady improvement in his breathing. Tube removed 6/5; follow-up film showed only trace residual fluid and no pneumothorax. Room air throughout, afebrile. Blood sugars acceptable on metformin.

Discharge medications: amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg twice daily for 7 more days. Resume home medications (metformin, atorvastatin, hydrochlorothiazide).
Allergies: ACE inhibitors (cough), sulfonamides (rash).

Follow-up: PCP within one week; repeat chest x-ray in 6 to 8 weeks to confirm resolution.

documents.title: Call from wife
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Patient's wife called: Scott was admitted Monday with fluid around his left lung after a pneumonia he had a couple of weeks ago (seen at an urgent care, we have no record of that visit). He has a chest tube in and is feeling better. Expected home Thursday or Friday. Scheduled hospital follow-up 6/10. Will request urgent care and hospital records.

orders.reason: confirm resolution of left parapneumonic effusion

documents.title: Hospital follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Home since Friday after 4 days in the hospital for a left pleural effusion following pneumonia. Pneumonia was diagnosed at an urgent care in mid-May; he finished a week of an antibiotic but can't remember which. In hospital: tap, then a chest tube for 2 days, IV antibiotics; home on amoxicillin-clavulanate, 3 days left. We don't have the discharge paperwork yet; going from his account and the hospital portal printout he brought.

Breathing close to normal, can do stairs at home, still tires by afternoon. Cough nearly gone. No fever. Lost a few pounds.

Exam: vitals as charted, comfortable on room air. Chest tube site clean, dressing off, no drainage. Left base slightly diminished breath sounds, no dullness I can appreciate. Right clear. Heart regular. No edema.

A/P
1. Left parapneumonic effusion, drained, improving. Finish amoxicillin-clavulanate. Chest x-ray late July to confirm it's cleared. Light duty at work for another week or two.
2. Pneumonia, treated.
3. Diabetes/HTN: continue metformin, HCTZ, atorvastatin. Labs at December visit.
Return sooner for fever, worsening breathing or chest pain.

documents.title: Hospital records received
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Discharge summary and ED record for 6/2-6/6 admission received from the hospital and filed. Urgent care office says their visit note will be faxed; not received. Routed to PCP.

reports.text: PA and lateral views. Lungs are clear. No pleural effusion; costophrenic angles sharp. Heart size and mediastinal contours normal. No pneumothorax.
reports.conclusion: Resolution of the previously seen left pleural effusion. No acute findings.

documents.title: Chest x-ray result
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Scott - your chest x-ray is clear. The fluid on the left side is completely gone and the lungs look normal. No further imaging needed.

documents.title: Immunizations
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Seasonal flu (L deltoid) and 2025-26 COVID (R deltoid). Patient feeling well. No reactions observed.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Routine check. Fully recovered from the summer's lung infection; back to full days. Weight back up. No gout. Admits holiday eating has started early.

Exam: vitals as charted. Lungs clear both bases. Heart regular. Feet normal sensation and pulses.

Plan: A1c, BMP, lipids, urine microalbumin. If A1c creeps much higher we'll talk about adding a second diabetes drug in the spring. Same meds for now. Return in 3 months.

documents.title: December labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Scott, A1c is close to target. Kidney function, potassium and cholesterol are fine; the urine protein is about where it has been. Let's recheck in March.

documents.title: Missed visit
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Left voicemail after no-show at 7:30 this morning. Called back at noon: forgot, a pour got moved up at one of his sites. Will call back to reschedule once his spring schedule settles.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, high MDM

orders.order: MRI brain with and without contrast
orders.reason: new progressive headaches with nausea and morning vomiting, age 60

documents.title: Follow-up
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Rescheduled from the March no-show. Wife came with him, mostly, she says, to make sure he mentions the headaches.

Headaches started about six weeks ago. Dull, both sides or more on the left, worst when he wakes and easing as the morning goes on. Queasy most mornings and has vomited a few times before breakfast. Acetaminophen takes the edge off. Never had headaches like this before. No fever, no neck stiffness, no vision change, no injury. Wife says he's been short with her and the crew lately, which isn't like him; he says it's the heat and the headaches. He denies weakness, numbness, trouble speaking or falls.

Exam: afebrile, vitals as charted. Alert, oriented, conversant, answers appropriately. Pupils equal and reactive, extraocular movements full, no nystagmus, face symmetric. Strength 5/5 in all four limbs, no pronator drift, reflexes symmetric, toes downgoing. Finger-nose and gait normal. Neck supple. Fundi not well seen through undilated pupils.

A/P
1. New, progressive headaches with morning predominance, nausea and vomiting at 60, with a personality change noticed by his wife. Nonfocal exam today, but this pattern needs imaging soon. Ordered an urgent MRI of the brain with gadolinium; prior auth submitted today. Told both of them plainly: any weakness, confusion, trouble talking, worsening vomiting or the worst headache of his life means go straight to the ED, don't wait for the MRI.
2. Diabetes: A1c and labs today.
3. HTN and lipids: no changes.
Will call with MRI scheduling.

documents.title: MRI authorization
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Insurance approved the brain MRI. Imaging center's first opening is Thursday 6/18 at 6:40 am. Called patient, confirmed the time, and repeated the ED precautions. He says the headaches are about the same.

documents.title: Labs
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Scott, Tuesday's blood work is reassuring: blood counts, kidney and liver tests and sodium are normal, and your A1c is close to target. Keep the MRI appointment on the 18th.

reports.text: Non-contrast CT of the head. Large mass in the left cerebral hemisphere with surrounding low density and mass effect, effacing the left lateral ventricle, with rightward midline shift. No acute hemorrhage. No hydrocephalus. Calvarium intact.
reports.conclusion: Large left hemispheric mass with midline shift. MRI with contrast recommended.

reports.study: MRI brain with and without contrast
reports.text: Multiplanar multisequence MRI of the brain before and after gadolinium. Large heterogeneous left hemispheric mass with thick, serpiginous rim enhancement surrounding central necrosis, extending across the corpus callosum to the opposite hemisphere in a butterfly configuration. Surrounding T2/FLAIR signal abnormality and mass effect with midline shift to the right. No other enhancing lesions.
reports.conclusion: Necrotic, enhancing left hemispheric mass crossing the corpus callosum (butterfly pattern), most consistent with a high-grade glial neoplasm.

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
Regional medical center ED. Seen 06/16/2026.

CC: headache and vomiting, now confused and weak on the right.

HPI: 60-year-old man with diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia and gout, last seen in this ED a year ago. Two months of worsening headache with nausea and vomiting. Over the past couple of weeks has had spells of confusion, and since yesterday his right arm and leg are weak. His wife says he has become more and more sluggish and irritable. He had an outpatient MRI booked for later this week.

Home meds (prior record): metformin 1000 mg BID, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily.
Allergies: ACE inhibitors (cough intolerance), sulfa drugs (rash).
FHx: brother melanoma, father T2DM, mother HTN.
Social: never smoker, no alcohol, construction site supervisor.

Exam: vitals reviewed. Awake and alert but looks exhausted. Right-sided hemiparesis, arm more than leg. Right Babinski sign present. Speech fluent.

Imaging: non-contrast head CT with a large left hemispheric mass and midline shift. MRI with contrast: heterogeneous, necrotic mass with serpiginous enhancement crossing the corpus callosum, butterfly pattern.

MDM: large left hemispheric mass with mass effect, imaging favoring a high-grade glioma. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV given. Neurosurgery consulted and accepts.

Disposition: admitted to neurosurgery.

reports.text: Specimen: brain, left hemisphere, mass, resection. Microscopic: highly cellular infiltrating astrocytic neoplasm with marked nuclear pleomorphism, brisk mitotic activity, microvascular proliferation and pseudopalisading necrosis. Immunohistochemistry: GFAP positive; IDH1 R132H negative; ATRX retained. Molecular: IDH1/IDH2 wild-type. MGMT promoter: methylated.
reports.conclusion: Glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, CNS WHO grade 4. MGMT promoter methylated.

reports.study: MRI brain with and without contrast
reports.text: Postoperative MRI within 72 hours of surgery. Expected postsurgical changes of left craniotomy and resection cavity. Residual nodular enhancing tumor along the margin and across the corpus callosum. Mass effect reduced compared with 06/16. No new hemorrhage of concern.
reports.conclusion: Subtotal resection with residual enhancing tumor crossing the corpus callosum.

procedures.procedure: Craniotomy with debulking of brain tumor

documents.title: Neurosurgery Discharge Summary
documents.author: neurosurgery
documents.body:
Admitted 06/16/2026, discharged 06/25/2026, neurosurgery service.

Principal diagnosis: glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4, left hemisphere crossing the corpus callosum.
Other: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, history of gout, history of stage IA melanoma (2021).

Course: admitted from the ED with a large left hemispheric mass and right hemiparesis. Dexamethasone 4 mg every 6 hours with improvement in headache and alertness. On 06/19 he underwent left craniotomy with debulking of the mass; because of extension across the corpus callosum a subtotal resection was the goal. Postoperative MRI on 06/20 showed residual enhancing tumor across the callosum and less mass effect. Pathology: glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, MGMT promoter methylated. Seen by neuro-oncology and radiation oncology in house; plan is standard radiation with concurrent temozolomide after wound healing. Right-sided weakness is somewhat better but persists. Blood sugars were followed closely while on steroids.

Discharge: home with his wife. Dexamethasone taper per the attached schedule. Resume home metformin, atorvastatin and blood pressure medication. No driving. Staples out at the neurosurgery clinic on day 10-14.

Follow-up: neurosurgery 2 weeks; neuro-oncology and radiation oncology to schedule chemoradiation.

documents.title: Call from wife
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Wife called from the hospital. Scott went to the ED yesterday afternoon with confusion and right arm and leg weakness. They found a large mass in the brain on CT and MRI and he's admitted to neurosurgery; surgery is being planned. She is understandably shaken. Let her know the PCP will be told right away. Cancelled Thursday's outpatient MRI with the imaging center since it was done in the hospital. Will request records.

documents.title: PCP call back
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Spoke with his wife at lunchtime. Told her how sorry I was and that we'd help however we can with whatever comes after the hospital. She'll call with updates; gave her the direct line.

documents.title: ED record received
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: ED note and imaging reports from 6/16 received from the hospital and filed. Discharge summary not yet available. Routed to PCP.

documents.title: Neuro-oncology consultation
documents.author: neuro-oncology
documents.body:
Cancer center neuro-oncology clinic. Visit date 07/14/2026.

Reason: newly diagnosed left hemispheric glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, WHO grade 4, MGMT promoter methylated, status post subtotal resection 06/19/2026.

He comes with his wife. Headaches are much better since surgery. Right-sided weakness persists, improving slowly with home exercises. No seizures. Tapering dexamethasone, now 2 mg daily.

Other history: type 2 diabetes, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, gout; stage IA melanoma of the back excised in 2021.
Medications per patient: metformin, atorvastatin, hydrochlorothiazide, dexamethasone taper.
Allergies: ACE inhibitors (cough), sulfonamide antibiotics (rash).

Exam: alert, oriented, speech normal. Right arm 4/5, right leg 4+/5. Incision healed.

Assessment and plan: we discussed the diagnosis and the standard treatment: radiation 60 Gy in 30 fractions with concurrent daily temozolomide 75 mg/m2, then adjuvant temozolomide cycles after a 4-week break. The methylated MGMT promoter predicts a better response to temozolomide. Chemoradiation is planned to start 07/20. Weekly blood counts during treatment. Taper dexamethasone off as tolerated. Return at the end of radiation, with MRI about 4 weeks after completion.

documents.title: Call from wife
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Wife called with an update. Surgery was June 19; pathology was a glioblastoma. He started radiation yesterday, every weekday for six weeks, along with a daily chemotherapy pill from the cancer center. She's driving him. He is still weak on the right but walking around the house. She asked for a metformin refill; mail order says the prescription is out of refills. We have not received the discharge summary or any cancer center notes; requested again.

documents.title: Refill
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Metformin 1000 mg twice daily, 90 days, sent to mail order. Asked RN to let the wife know I'm available by phone and will reach out to the neuro-oncology team once their notes arrive.

documents.body: Neurosurgery discharge summary, operative note and pathology from the 6/16-6/25 admission received on third request. Filed. Routed to PCP.
